Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 128, to amend an Act to incorporate the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners.
He said: This Bill is to amend a Bill that was introduced and enacted into legislation at the last session of the House in regard to the harbour of Vancouver. The amendment is being made at the request of the harbour commissioners. Under the provisions of that Bill the rental derived from the leases of the foreshore of the harbour were paid over to the harbour commissioners and authority was given to the harbour commissioners to deal with the foreshore in the future. But their powers were limited to making leases for a period of twenty-one years with renewals for further periods of twenty-one years each. It has been found by the harbour commissioners that this provision is not altogether workable, that there are certain cases in which they feel it is more in the interest of the harbour that, instead of leasing the foreshares, there should be power to make grants of them. Therefore, it is proposed to revest the power of dealing with these foreshores in the Governor in Council under a provision that before the Governor in Council deals with any of them he shall first of all get a report from the harbour commissioners embodying their views and recommendations in regard to the matter. This is in order to make the Act workable and it is done at the suggestion of the harbour commissioners who found that the Act in this respect was not as elastic and workable as they would have liked to have it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. CARROLL moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 129, respecting hours of service of railway employees.
He said: The chief provision of this Bill limits the number of hours of service which a railway corporation shall demand of its officials to fourteen a day, and specifies the period that must be allowed the employees for rest betweeen the working hours. Clause 3 of the Bill states the hours of service that cannot be exceeded by order of 1381
any railway company and fully sets forth the hours of duty and off duty that shall be required or permitted. It is careful to make exception in eases of accidental obstruction over which the company, or its agents, has no control. It sets these forth in detail. The main purpose of this clause is to provide a law that can be invoked in case the regulations set forth therein are violated in any way, which law must be interpreted by a judicial tribunal, from whose judgment there is this appeal, thus giving thereto that elasticity which the changes of condition from time to time may demand. The fixing of the hours of service by any body, such as the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, for example, would mean cast iron rules lacking that elasticity and from which no appeal is obtainable. It is quite obvious that this protection is in the interest not only of the employees affected thereby but also of the rail-way companies and of the general public. The clause which provides for the offence on the part of the railway company and the penalty attached thereto ; it also provides for the prosecution of a suit in civil courts in case of violation. The general intention of the Bill is to protect railway employees, and to protect the companies from accidents and the general public from suffering injury and damage by these accidents which frequently occut.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first
time.

investigation. There were debates in this House. During the whole course of these debates and investigations it was very-palpable that the Government of the day was endeavouring to keep from the public throughout Canada the actual facts in regard to the extravagance, recklessness and mismanagement which attended the building of the Transcontinental railway. No wonder that the Government changed. The Government having lost the confidence of the people, the people decided in favour of a change of Government. One of the first steps that the new Government took, in carrying out the pledge which its leader made to the people, was to appoint a royal commission to see whether or not the complaints which that party had made in the past were true, and, if true, whether the party which was responsible for the whole transaction from its inception, and whose recklessness and extravagance are shown in this report, was culpable or deserving of the severe censure of the House and of the country. It has been shown by the result to have been more blameworthy than the two commissioners who have made this report, and who deserve the thanks of a grateful country for giving the facts to the people.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), who moved this resolution, sat on these benches for many years as Minister of Railways and Canals, and he was familiar with what was going on. He was repeatedly asked for information. Sometimes he gave it, sometimes he did not give it, and sometimes the hon. gentleman gave information which, I think, from a reading of the speech which he delivered on Tuesday and Wednesday last, he would be very sorry indeed to-day to realize that he had given to the House. The hon. gentleman presented himself to the electors at BTOckville for re-election as Minister of Railways and Canals, and went down to defeat upon a policy advocated by his leader, .a policy which had for its object the absolute destruction of the utility of the Transcontinental railway, and the diversion of traffic from it to north and south lines.
We, the Conservative party of Canada, complained, and we complained early. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had hardly got his breath after making that memorable speech on the 30th of July, 1903, before the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), then leader of the

Opposition, made a speech, for the preparation of which there could be very little time, in which he outlined certain strong features which might appear to be of very great import to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and to the Government of which he was then the leader. The first question, which was of very serious import to the country, but which did not appear to be of very serious import to my right hon. friend or his Government, was what this great undertaking, for the beginning of which even time would not wait, was going to cost, and how great was to be the burden that it would put upon the people of the country. What did my right hon. friend say? Was my right hon. friend serious when he told this House that the railway from Moncton to Winnipeg would cost $13,000,000 and not a cent more? These are his absolute words. Nobody believed it. Nobody took him seriously. He did not take himself seriously. He launched this project upon the people without the slightest consideration what the cost was going to be or what would be the burden which would be imposed upon the ratepayers. Across the floor of this House the then leader of the Opposition, now the leader of the Government, sent the challenge to the ministers of the Crown that they were unable to tell him the cost of this gigantic undertaking within $10,090,000. My right hon. friend gave sufficient opportunity for a reply, but not one of them rose. Not in connection with that, but in connection with another charge that he was confronted with, namely, that there was no information upon which to base an estimate of the cost, my right hon. friend replied: We Rave 'mountains 'of information,' abundance of maps, plans by provincial Governments, and reports upon everything, but the fact remains that this project was launched without one single statement from any scientific gentleman having reference to the nature of the territory which was to be traversed by this railway, or showing how *much this railway would cost per mile.
I confront the leader of the Opposition now with his words-$13,000,000 and no more. I emphasize that with the Liberal pamphlet which was published in the election of 1904 giving the cost of the Transcontinental railway at $13,000,000, and I ask my right hon. friend whether, in his judgment, and having regard to the uncontrovertible and uncontradictable '

facts, as they now appear in this report, he was not misleading the people of Canada at that time and was not intending to mislead them to the point that the people would be committed to the Tailway, and would have to have it carried through.
Another estimate as to the cost of the road was furnished by my right hon. friend's Minister of Finance at that time- a very careful estimate, Mt. Speaker. It created the impression in the House that the estimate which Mir. Fielding gave of $61,415,000 for the construction of the Moncton to Winnipeg section was most liberal. He wrote a letter in connection with that which is shown in the exhibits, and which I must ask the House to listen to because it is distinctly interesting. Under date of May 11, 1904, and after the minister had made a speech upon the subject, he wrote this letter:
Ottawa, May 11, 1914.
Dear Mr. Emmerson,
Last summer, while I was acting Minister of Railways, and when the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme came up, I asked Mr. Schreiber's opinion as to the probable cost of constructing the eastern division (Government portion) of the road. Mr. Schreiber gave me the information, although not in the form of a written report, and I used it in the House, mentioning his name as my authority. His opinion was that a road could be constructed from Quebec to Moncton for $25,000 per mile, and from Quebec to Winnipeg for $28,000 per mile.
These estimates were made for a road of an ordinary character such as is constructed elsewhere. In order to make a sufficiently liberal allowance for a road of better character, I added 25 per cent, making the estimate $31,250 per mile from Quebec to Moncton, and $35,000 per mile from Quebec to Winnipeg. I have not spoken to Mr. Schreiber on the matter of late, but from other experienced railway men I have received assurances that my estimate was a, most liberal one and that the road could probably be constructed well within these figures.
As above stated, I did not obtain a written report from Mr. Schreiber. I think it might be convenient to have a report from him. May I suggest that you discuss the matter with him, and, if there is no objection, ask him to make a short memorandum, putting in writing the information which he gave me last summer. Yours faithfully,
(Sgd) W. S. Fielding. Honourable H. R. Emmerson,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa, Ont.
And $61,415,000 was stated by the Minister of Finance to this House and to this country, as being a most liberal estimate, based upon the information furnished and assurances given by experienced railway men- men, for instance, like M. P. Davis, who undoubtedly would not mislead the minister in regard to any additional amount that
would be taken from the people for the construction of this railway.
The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in a most eloquent speech; a speech more eloquent than convincing to the thoughtful and earnest reader, expressed great concern that no delay should take place in the immediate construction of this much-needed railway. And yet our friends opposite are attempting to alarm Canada because there has been a large expenditure in developing transportation facilities under conditions that are an absolute necessity if that development is even measurably to be * achieved.
I am not going to disregard or ignore the necessities of the treasury; I should be sorry to advocate waste in any degree. But if it is true that the Transcontinental railway has cost, or will cost $200,000,000, yet if by that expenditure we are able to do for the development of the Prairie West what could not otherwise be done, then it is a wise and economical expenditure, beyond any question. Hon. gentlemen opposite are spending money for transportation facilities. They are spending $50,000,000 in deepening the Welland canal. Will they count the interest on that from to-day until some time in the distant future for the purpose of alarming the people of Canada as to the cost of that great work? Surely not. Yet, for whom is the Welland canal being deepened? It is being deepened for the glory of Canada, but, in some degree, we hope, for the benefit of Canada. But it is being deepened just as much for the benefit of the transportation and production interests of the United States as for those of

Canada. Surely, these hon. gentlemen who glory in the fact that they are spending $50,000,000 in a transportation enterprise which will be at least half for the benefit of that country with whom they do not wish truck or trade, are not the people to complain because there is an expenditure of $50,000,000, or $100,000,000 if you like, in the construction of a line of railway that is located solely within Canada for the benefit of Canada, not only in the production of its wheat fields of the prairies, but just as much for the development of its trade passing through its own ports on the Atlantic seaboard. And without such a road there could not be adequate development either of the prairie wheatfields or of the Atlantic ports.
I have said that the increase of production in the West depends upon the possibilities of production-upon the conditions of soil and climate, the cost of the land, the cost of living of the man who works the land, and the cost of the machinery with which he works the land. But it depends also upon the cost of getting the product to the market. Now, in regard to that question of marketing the crop, before the Grand Trunk Pacific project was instituted, and since that time, there has been almost every year in the West what is called a grain blockade. Our grain, on being harvested, (was sent forward to the head of the lakes, and as much of dt as could be transported across the lakes during the same summer was so transported. The rest remained on the farmers' hands or dealers' hands or in the terminal elevators until the following spring. That means that under conditions that then prevailed it was the business of every	farmer to	get	his grain out	in thefall.	By doing	so	he not only	savedinterest on money he may have owed, but he saved the carrying charges on that grain until	the next	spring. The elevatorcharges are one cent a bushel a month, so upon every bushel of grain that was held in the country there was 'a loss to the producer of a minimum of five cents. But besides that, in the rush, the attempt of every man to get his grain marketed in order to save that five cents, there ensued year	after year	a	condition of	grain
blockade which increased the loss, because the buyer, unable to get the grain he had brought forwarded to the lakes because of the shortage of cars, had to discount the possibility, and hammered down the price

accordingly.	So that at the least, the
farmer who did not get hisi grain forwarded in the fall lost five cents a bushel for storage charges, and if he were compelled to sell he possibly lost five cents more on account of the condition of blockade which existed before the close of navigation. Suppose a crop of 100,000,000 bushels, of iwhich 50,000,000 could go forward in the fall of its growth, and figuring that 50,000,000 must remain behind, there would be an absolute loss of 5 cents a bushel on the second 50,000,000 bushels, with a possible loss of 10 cents a bushel on the whole or a part, according to the more or less serious character of the blockade. So there would be a minimum loss of $2,500,000, and a possible loss of $5,000,000 or even more-as we certainly had in the year 1911. Now, there is only one cure for that condition, and that is to have railway transportation from the wheat fields to the ocean ports all the year round. But, you may say: This last year you had not any grain blockade, you had the largest crop you ever had, and yet the railways were able to handle the crop, and it went forward without any blockade to the lake ports, in fact three-fourths of the marketable crop found the world's market before the close of navigation. If those conditions were repeated every year there would be no need of talking about a blockade. The conditions were exceptional last year; the crop was early, with light straw, easily threshed, there were favourable weather conditions and the railroads were more fully equipped than they ever had been before. But, it will be said, another year may be just as good; why do you argue that there must be rail communication with the western wheat fields all the year round when by existing facilities you get your grain out without the difficulty and loss of blockade? Here is the condition that we face now. Our production has increa"ed greatly; our export last fall was 90,000,000 bushels, the larger part of which, was thrown on the Liverpool market within three months, the result being that the price of Manitoba wheat was hammered down from three to six cents a bushel. So that we now have a new condition; we have overcome a blockade, but we are as badly off as ever, for with our enormous production thrown on the market at one time the price is hammered down and the loss is practically the same as in the case of the grain blockade. There is the condition: we lose by reason of storage if the grain does not go forward; we lose by reason of blockade if the car supply
is short, and we lose toy reason of the depression of the world's prices if every condition is favourable. Again I say there is only one remedy for this, and that is rail communication from the wheat fields to the Atlantic ports,'so that the grain can be sent forward as the market demands, and so that there shall be no grain blockade, no payment for winter storage, and no slackening of the world's prices. Say we shipped
90,000,000 bushels last fall, and that one-third of it went forward without injuring the world's price; I have it on the best of authority that on at least 60,000,000 bushels of our crop of last year the farmers-because it all comes back to them-lost from four to six cents a bushel because of that wheat being thrown on the Liverpool market within a very short space of time. That is to say, the farmers of the West, in this year of hard times, lost $3,000,000 in cold cash because of that condition. It was to overcome that condition that this Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise was placed before the people of Canada as it was, in the year that it was, and with all the needs and the urgent conditions that were set out in the speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister of that day. Every word and every line of that speech has been justified and more than justified by the events since that time.
We had a line of railway between the wheatfields and the Canadian Atlantic ports, but it was a matter of railroad knowledge and it was a matter of business knowledge that that railroad was so constructed that it could not handle the crop at a profit to both the railroad and the producer. The distance was too great, the grades were too heavy, the cutvos were too short. If that crop of the West is to be handled as it should be handled, by rail carriage all the year round, then it must be by some other railroad built on. the shortest line from point to point, with the .lowest .possible gradients and the slightest possible curves, so that there shall be the least possible distance to cover and the lowest possible cost in covering that distance. It may be that, after all has been done, the purpose .still may not be achieved, but it was the business of the Government of that day, or of any day, to use the resources of the Dominion of Canada according to their best judgment, in whatever amount was necessary, in order to achieve that result. My hon. friend who has just spoken, and the same assertion has been made and repeated by other speakers, said that this project was presented to the House before therf

was sufficient information with regard to the country that it was to go through. I can only say that the last rail has been laid between Winnipeg and Moncton and it is a fact that the distance of the rails between those cities is the shortest that oould be obtained. It is a fact that between Winnipeg and Quebec there is not a gradient over the maximum allowed by the agreement, except where this Government, for the purpose of destroying the object of the road, has deliberately and contrary to the agreement with the Grand Trunk, put in such grades.
I am under the impression that there is a general belief that the late Government set out to do the impossible when they undertook to build a line from the wheat-fields to the Atlantic ports that would compete with the lines to United States ports, and that such a line would be impracticable for the economic carriage of grain. Just on that point, allow me to give the figures. From Winnipeg to St. John by way of the National Transcontinental to Chipman, allowing seventy-five miles from there to St. John, which is the actual rail distance, the distance is 1,825 miles. . It is eighty miles shorter than the Canadian Pacific railway route from Winnipeg to St. John; sixty miles longer than the Canadian Pacific railway route from Winnipeg by way of Montreal to Boston, one hundred miles longer than the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific railway routes by way of Winnipeg, Cochrane and Montreal to Portland, fifteen miles longer than via the Grand Trunk to Montreal and New York. While it is true that there is some disadvantage as far as the route to Portland, is concerned, the Transcontinental is still within competitive range.; on a distance of 1,800 miles, one hundred miles more is not such a tremendous difference. When in addition to the facts as to mileage you take into consideration that on every mile of the 1,825 miles of the Transcontinental a load can be hauled at an absolutely minimum cost, and that it is the only road of that class that reaches any of these ports. I think it will be admitted that so far as competition is concerned, we have certainly provided an efficiently competitive railway for the carriage of grain from Winnipeg to St. John able to compete with the route to any American port, including Portland.

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

When the House rose at six o'clock. Mr. Speaker, I was giving the distances over the eastern section of the National Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to St. John and comparing them with the distances from Winnipeg to United States ports by way of the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway. From that statement it was apparent that the distance was somewhat greater to St. John than to Portland, Boston and New York. It is a fact, however, that a moderate difference in distance does not control the direction of freight traffic, as can be seen in the ease of the Canadian Pacific railway which hauls wheat from Fort William to St. John although the route is 140 miles farther than the haul would be from Fort William through Montreal to Boston. It shows that railways are not governed absolutely by actual distances. However, leaving that aside, it must be apparent that the distance is greater to St. John than to the United States ports of New York, Boston and Portland. If it were possible to bring Portland, Boston or New York under Canadian jurisdiction, to make these ports a part of the Dominion of Canada, by any means, or at any reasonable expense, that would be one thing that might be done. Another thing that might be done would be to leave matters as they are- leave our Maritime ports and provinces without competitive railway connection with the prairie provinces, practically treating these provinces and ports as though they were not a part of the business life and interest of the Dominion ; leave them, as they have been ever since they have been a part of the Dominion, so to speak, on the sidetrack. We may suppose that one of these things might have been done. Failing the possibility of making the United States ports Canadian ports, we take issue with the position of our friends on the other side of the House, as set forth by their statement at the inception of the scheme, and quite as strongly in the debate which has been proceeding in the House during the past few days in support of the specific declaration by their duly appointed commissioners that the section of the National Transcontinental railway east of Quebec should not have been built and that it was a waste of public money to build it. We support and justify the position of the late Government which used the resources of this country to build a line of railway from Winnipeg, by way of Quebec, to St. John

by the shortest possible route and with the best advantages as to grades, curves and improvements in transportation generally. To do that costs money; it costs a great deal of money, but I submit it is worth something to the Dominion of Canada to have our winter ports and our Maritime provinces linked up practicably and profitably by railway connection with the prairie provinces and the Pacific coast. As to the amount of money that has been spent, let it be great or let it be small; if Canada is to be a country all parts must be properly connected so that business can be transacted by one part with the other. By giving railway transportation, as has been done bv the construction of the Transcontinental railway, the industries of the Maritime provinces are given access to the markets of the prairies just as the producers of the prairies are given access to the markets of the world through the Martime provinces' ports by the construction of this line on the scale on which it has been constructed, and these provinces, for the first time in the history of the Dominion have become, or will become, part and parcel of the general business of the country.
If it is established, as it is, that we have provided an efficiently competitive route through our own winter ports, as compared with competitive winter ports in the United States, the question arises: can such a route, having been constructed, compete efficiently and satisfactorily with water transportation as it exists at the present time ? I know it is taken for granted that it cannot. It is assumed that there is no possibility of rail transportation competing with wateT transportation as we have it at the present time. This is a matter that will bear some consideration, and first let me disabuse the House of the idea that we get the benefit of the present system of water, or water and rail, transportation as a free gift. Take Winnipeg as the starting point. I find that it costs six cents to take a bushel of wheat from Winnipeg to Fort William. May I say right here, that that is the standard rate upon which all the grain export rates over the whole of the railway systems in the three prairie provinces is based. We get our wheat from Winnipeg for six cents. It costs three-quarters of a cent to clean it, elevate it and store it for fifteen days. It then costs anywhere from two to six cents to take it across the lakes from Fort William to Midland. Six cents, of course, is an abnormal rate. That was the highest point reached in 1912, which was a year
of high rates; but let us assume that the rates will range from two to six cents. It may have gone below two cents at some time, but that is rare, and the lower rate need not be considered seriously. At Midland there is another elevator charge of one-half cent, and then there is the rail charge from Midland to Montreal, varying from three to four and one-half cents including the elevator charge at Montreal. It costs us twelve and one-quarter cents to land a bushel of grain from Winnipeg in Montreal. Twelve and one-quarter cents is the minimum charge with the possible maximum of seventeen and three-quarter cents. The recent arrangement in regard to transportation. on the upper lakes tendts to insure that the purely lake rate will increase rather than diminish.
Why?

Because of the shipping
combine. The combine is formed to enable them to raise the rates, and if they do not raise the rates their purpose would, fail.

Another company is being
formed.

This company having raised the rates abnormally, an opening is given for another company to be formed, but the purpose of this shipping combine on the lakes is to raise the rates to the highest posssible limit, and, therefore, we must look, not for a reduction of the lake rates under present conditions, but rather for an increase. We land our wheat at Montreal, from Winnipeg, at from twelve and one-quarter cents to seventeen and one-quarter cents. I am speaking now about the use of the winter ports, and, therefore we must add five months storage, on that part of the crop that does not go forward in the season of its production; that is, the part of the crop that would be'available for transportation by the all-rail winter route to St. John. We have a minimum rate therefore of twelve and one-quarte'- cents carriage and five cents storage, or seventeen and one-quarter cents on all the wheat that does not come forward in the season of its production. As to the all-rail haul to St. John, the standard rate from Winnipeg to Fort William for the 419 miles is six cents a bushel. I have heard some very finely drawn calculations as to the cost of transportation, but I will take this rate of six cents for the 419 miles, which is the standard rate for the wheat transportation in the West.
Is six cents the rate paid last season to the Grand Trunk Pacific and to the Canadian Pacific railway and to the Canadian Northern railway?
Yes, ftiat is the rate that was fixed.
By the three companies?
It was fixed by an arrangement between the Government and the Canadian Pacific railway in 1897, and it has prevailed ever since.
It is a uniform rate?

Yes, and on that rate the transportation of wheat throughout the West is based* It is not always the same rate per mile, because as the distance increases the rate decreases, but it is the basis. The distance from Winnipeg to St. John is four and one-third times as great as the distance from Winnipeg to Fort William, and, therefore, at the very most, the charge for hauling grain that distance should not be more than four and one-third times more than the rate from Winnipeg to Fort William, or twenty-six cents per bushel. The rate from Winnipeg to Fort William was fixed when the railroad from Winnipeg to Fort William was in its original low-class condition; the Canadian Pacific railway had not then been improved and double-tracked. That was then considered to be a profitable rate for haul over a railroad that was what must be called a low standard road; the original Canadian Pacific line from Fort William to Winnipeg was built on the standard of that day, when a one per cent grade was considered to be a very good grade.

In what way was the
Grand Trunk Pacific brought into any arrangement to charge a particular rate from Winnipeg? I understood that when the Grand Trunk' Pacific was constructed, the rate would be reduced. Is the Grand TruYik Pacific in any way bound to that fixed rate by an arrangement between the late Government and the Canadian Pacific railway?

Certainly not; but as my hon. friend knows, all the railway companies are now under the control of the Railway Commission, and they, of course, naturally will charge all that the Railway Commission will let them charge. This original arrangement, between the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Government, with regard to the rate from Winnipeg to Fort William, 
has been approved by the Railway Commission, and therefore the railways competing over that route charge the same rate.
Then there is no competition at all.

There is no competition
at all in rates.
But they could charge a lower rate if they wanted to?

Certainly they could, but we are not to assume that they want to, or that they ever will want to; that would be expecting too much. The Grand Trunk Pacific will charge whatever the Railway Commission will let them charge. We instituted a Railway Commission for the purpose of placing a control upon rates, so that they may be fixed with due regard for the investment in the enterprise, and the interest of the customers of the road.
Does the hon. member say that the Railway Commission had nothing to do with fixing the rate on wheat between Winnipeg and Fort William?

That rate was fixed long before the Railway Commission came into existence, but the Railway Commission has approved of that rate as it stands to-day. To-morrow, the Railway Commission may reduce it, but they have not seen fit to do so. At all events, it was possible to carry grain for that distance over the kind of low-grade road that existed when the rate was put into effect. There is evidence that a railroad of the standard of the Grand Trunk Pacific, as specified in the contract between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Government, has a capacity practically double that of a road of the standard of the Canadian Pacific railway between Winnipeg and Fort William, at the time this arrangement was made. The Grand Trunk Pacific could haul wheat 419 miles on their line between Winnipeg and Fort William for one-half the cost the Canadian Pacific railway could haul it over their line from Winnipeg to Fort William, with the Canadian Pacific railway line in the condition it was when the arrangement was made.
Why do they not do it and show to the people that they are willing to give low rates?
I have been pointing out that they will do so only when they are compelled to.
I understood you had made an arrangement with them that they would be compelled to carry grain at the cheapest rate.

We made an arrangement with them to build a road for them over which they would be able to carry at the cheapest possible rate, but at the same time we established the Railway Commission with authority to control rates, having due regard to the interests of both parties to the transaction. We do not expect the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, any more than the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or any other railway company, to carry at any less rate than the Railway Commission will compel them to.
We have built them a railroad that will enable them to carry traffic at half the actual cost of transportation that it would have cost the Canadian Pacific railway for the distance of 419 miles at the time the Canadian Pacific railway agreed to carry at 6 cents a bushel. I maintain that, with the road of the standard that is being constructed, if 6 cents a bushel was a fair rate from Winnipeg to Fort William, over the Canadian Pacific railway as it was then constructed, half that rate for each section of 419 miles would be a fair rate between Winnipeg and St. John. In other words 26 cents would be the same rate; the half of 26 cents or 13 cents would be an equally good grain rate, compared with what the Canadian Pacific railway has been and is receiving. I am not suggesting that the Grand Trunk Pacific should be compelled to carry at that rate. It is a theoretical rate. In my judgment, however, it would be fair that the Railway Commission should compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry grain from Winnipeg to St. John over such a line, as we promised to give, and as we gave them as long as we were there to do so, at one-third less than the rate that I have mentioned. That is to say, according to the calculation I have made and the figures I have given, the Grand Trunk Pacific can carry and should be compelled to carry grain from Winnipeg to St. John, if everything be worked out as it should be, for 17J cents a bushel as against a lakeland-rail route, with winter storage, of 17i cents a bushel as at present existing. I think I have absolutely proved that, if this railroad be finished as we intended to finish it, we shall have thereby established at any rate a competitive route by which it should not cost more to carry grain in
the winter time than the minimum cost to hold grain during the winter and transport it by lake and rail in the summer; but by having that all-rail route at that rate, we have a means of regulating the charges by way of lake and rail as they exist at present. I gave the minimum rate; but the maximum rate without storage by lake and rail is equal to the all-rail rate to St. John that I have given.

Do I understand that
the 6-cent rate charged by the Canadian Pacific railway is fixed, so that it cannot be changed by the Board of Railway Commissioners?

No, the commissioners
could cut that down. They certainly could do so so far as the Grand Trunk is concerned.
I mean the Canadian Pacific railway.

I do not know whether
they could do so in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway, because a bargain was made.
It is the first time I have heard that point raised.

But I am sure that,
whatever rate the Grand Trunk charges, it is absolutely under the control of the Railway Commission. If we can get that all-the-year-round rate, we are absolutely relieved from the two conditions of grain blockade in the fall and of slump on the Liverpool market by reason of the grain being rushed forward in a very short period. As I have pointed out, that means on the present crop of the Northwest anywhere from $2,500,000 to $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 in the year. Of course, as the crop increases, that benefit will increase correspondingly. The present Government is well aware of the injurious conditions that have existed in past times because of grain blockades. It is because of these grain blockades that they propose to establish interior terminal elevators. They have now under contract three of those elevators at a cost of $4,500,000, hoping thereby to minimize to some extent the injury resulting from the annual recurrent grain blockade. We say that if they will complete the Grand Trunk Pacific as it was intended to be completed, the question of blockade will be solved without the erection of interior terminal elevators, and the still more serious question of the depression of the Liverpool market by

throwing our crop on that market in a month or two will be -done away with also. The construction of that railway over the route over which it is .being constructed and under the physical conditions under which it was to be constructed, is the solution of the problem of the export of Canada's grain so far as that problem can be solved by the action of this Government. Whatever derogates from those conditions in lengthening the road, in degrading it, in militating against the abilitity of the company to finance, is all a blow at the welfare, progress and prosperity of our western prairie country and of this whole Dominion, because I think it is borne in the mind of every man in Canada to-day that it is upon the next crop in the Northwest and upon the prices that shall be received for that crop that this country depends for help in its present condition.
Will the hon. gentleman say, whether or not, in his opinion, if that road were constructed for $100,000,000 less than it is costing, that would enable the road to give better freight rates?
Most undoubtedly. If the road could be built of the same standard as it is now and of the .same length for $100,000,000 less, undoubtedly-
Or for $40,000,000 less?

Yes, for $10,000,000 less, it would make it possible for the Railway Commission to insist upon a correspondingly lower freight rate. We admit that freely; but, of course, we also maintain that, no matter how cheaply the road is built, unless it has the short mileage and the low grade, it cannot do. the business at the price. We have that condition illustrated right alongside the Grand Trunk railway to-day; we have the Canadian Northern railway, built, I am sure the House will agree, cheaply enough, built so as to fake advantage of velocity grades wherever they could be put in, and certainly not restricted as to length of line or curves. But I have yet to learn that the problem of transportation of Canada's grain crop is going to be solved by the Canadian Northern railway; nor am I informed that the country is going to have the benefit of the operation of this line without a very serious cost.

I am informed that the Canadian Northern railway took out nearly
40,000,000 bushels of the Canadian grain

crop last year at the current rate. You do not deny that?
No.
There was no kick about the rates?
No.
Then it is helping.

It is certainly helping. We are not finding fault with the Canadian Northern railway, nor with what it has done as a western road lin bringing grain to the head of the lakes. But I have been trying for an hour and a half to point out to the House that it was very far from . being the solution of our problem of grain marketing; that we had to have a better condition than prevails to-day between the head of the lakes and the ocean or we could not get that return on our labour,
' that profit on our production that would enable us to increase our production and thereby make Canada great and prosperous. I am showing now that in that part of the Canadian Northern railway which is paralleling the Grand Trunk railway you have the very condition that hon. gentlemen opposite have insisted should prevail on the Grand Trunk railway. But they do not find the results that we would like to see on the Grand Trunk railway, nor do they find the financial advantage that they would seem to insist.would accrue provided we had a low-class road instead of a high-class road.
Now, I may point out that there is not only the matter of transportation of grain during the winter that is giving us an all-the-year-round outlet, but there is the matter of transportation of grain in the summer. I find that the mileage on the Transcontinental, between Winnipeg and Quebec which is a tide-water port, is only 1,344 miles. Reckoning on the same basis as I gave for the rates from Winnipeg to St. John, I take it that from Winnipeg to Quebec all-rail would be 20 cents a bushel. But if that were reduced by one-third, as I claim it might be, we should have a 13} all-rail all-the-year-round rate between Winnipeg and Quebec, as against a summer lake-and-rail rate as at present between Fort William and Montreal of a minimum of 12} and a maximum of 17 cents. Now, I do not *or a moment expect that grain will be hauled from the prairies to Quebec during the season of export in the fall. When the rush of grain is on, it will no doubt be taken to the head of lake Superior, as much of it

as can be sent forward. But we will have an all-rail route to Quebec that will be able to regulate and control and keep within reasonable limits the rates across' the lakes; and the experience of the last three or four years is that we need sonre such means of keeping down these lake-and-rail charges. If there were no means of controlling these lake charges, as I have said, they could be put up as high as 17 cents.

I think that was only
in the fall of the year.
Mr. OLIVER. Certainly. But we do not want to be up against a proposition like that if it can be avoided. Just as the New York Central railway from Buffalo to New York, running alongside the Erie canal and the Hudson river, has an important effect not only in actually transporting the grain but in keeping the rates at a reasonable figure, so, I maintain, the Transcontinental between Winnipeg and Quebec will have an important and salutary effect in controlling the summer export rates of grain, and just as, I believe, the railroad from Winnipeg to St. John will have a beneficial effect in providing a winter outlet at reasonable rates. Thus, we have the advantage of this road both in summer and in winter. And, as I have said, the project if carried to completion is an important solution of the great problem that has to be faced by the producers of the West, a problem that, unless it can be solved, must certainly prevent the full development of this country. Our competitors in the wheat markets of the world are many, but particularly Argentina and Australia, two great countries where there are vast areas of unoccupied land available to be brought under wheat production. Unless we can land our product at a figure to compete, we shall be put out of business so far as producing wheat for the world's market is concerned. We must realize that we are not the only people producing wheat in the world; we are not the only country that has cheap land and lots of it. There is a life-and-death competition between the Argentine, Australia and Canada, and unless Canada is prepared to get into the market on more favourable terms, utilizing her shorter distance from the market, the other countries will take the market and we shall have to consider ourselves out of it.
I wish to make some allusion to the question of capitalization. Admitting that we have the short distance, admitting that we have a high-class road, it is nevertheless the fact that if we have excessive overcapitalization, we cannot get the full benefit of the character of road that we have built.
It has been the pleasing task of out friends on the other side to declare broadly and persistently and to attempt to prove that the capital charges to be carried by the Transcontinental are such as to preclude competitive carriage of wheat. The fact i3 this: the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to St. John is to cost, everything paid, interest charges and all, a trifle over $100,000 a mile, upon which interest is to be paid at 3 per cent. That is the only capital charge against the road that has to be considered when the rates are being fixed by the Railway Commission'-a Charge of $3,000 a mile. The Union Pacific has a capital charge of $150,000 a mile, and they pay on that captial charge an interest of say 4 per cent. In other words, while the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to St. John will carry $3,000 a mile capital charge, the Union Pacific carries $6,000 a mile capital charge. The Southern Pacific, with a capitalization of $140,000 a mile, at 4 per cent will carry $5,600 a mile capital charge. The Canadian Pacific is carrying a capital charge of $46,000 a mile. Canadian' Pacific stock is worth over 200; in other words, the Canadian Pacific is paying dividends on a capital charge of over $100,000 a mile at a rate not less than 4 per cent. It may be said that what other roads can do, under less favourable conditions the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, operating the Transcontinental, will not be able to do, and that our country will not progress sufficiently to give the business that will enable the company to make this interest. I am sorry that our friends have iso little confidence in the country or in the success of their policy and administration as to believe that there is not to be sufficient increase of business to provide traffic for this road. I have confidence enough in the country to believe that, given a proper .administration of the country's business and a proper completion and administration of this road, it will not be a question of getting enough traffic for the road to carry, but it will be a question of the road carrying the traffic that will be there for it. One would imagine from the attitude of our friends on the other side that no further development i3 to be expected in this country. I remember very well that after the Canadian Pacific railway was completed it was broadly declared that there was no need for any more railroads in Canada-that the development

of the country was completed. In fact, I heard my friend the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) the other night say that it was gross impertinence and mere vanity on the part of the Liberal, Government that they undertook to 'build a transcontinental line at all. I find that there has been some increase in railroad business in Canada. In 1903 the railroads carried 47,000,000 tons of freight and in 1913 they carried 106,000,000 tons of freight. In 1903 they carried 22,000,000 passengers and in 1913 they carried 46,000,000 passengers. I have every confidence in the belief that the limit of the growth of this country has not been reached and that the maximum amount of business to be done by our railroads has not been attained. I think there is every reason to believe that the Grand Trunk Pacific will find the business to handle and will be able to do the business at a profit to the company, and to the benefit of the country.
In looking through the blue-books to-day I ran across some figures in the matter of comparative cost that I am going to intrude into this discussion, merely for the purpose of information. I find that 18,000,000 acres of land were given as a part of the aid to the first great transcontinental railroad built by the Dominion, and that 11,000,000 acres of that land have been sold, bringing a return of $75,000,000. The company still have
7,300,000	acres to sell, and at the rate at which land has sold for the past three years, about $13 an acre, their 7,000,000 acres of selected land ought to be worth to them $91,000,000. So that when it comes to a question of aid to railways, our hon. friends on the other side can, I think, claim the merit of liberality even beyond what they are willing to concede to us in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific.
I will deal only for a short time with some of the allusions that have been made by our friends on the other side. I wish to speak particularly of this assertion to be found on page 24 of the report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton:
We unhesitatingly find that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, instead of discountenancing, has rather encouraged this inexperienced commission in its extravagant expenditure on this railway.
That is a very serious charge to make against a responsible business enterprise. Instead of bearing out that assertion, the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) to-day drew the attention of the House to a communication addressed by Mr. Hays, president of the Grand Trunk Pacific, to the then Government, asking that a certain con-

I find also that the Grand Trunk Pacific as a construction company took four contracts. In these four contracts they were $958,000 less than the next lowest bidder, so that instead of the road having cost more because of the Grand Trunk Pacific having entered the field as contractors, it cost nearly a million dollars less in the case of these four contracts. The Davis' put up their deposit money; they assigned their contract; and this Government made the final payments upon that contract. My hon. friend the Solicitor General says that the late commission, by resolution, relieved the contractor from payment of the penalty. If it .is intended" as a reflection on the business methods employed in the construction of the road, then I have this to say: In the first place, un ler the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Pacific as lessees of the Government, had the right-the obligation was placed upon them-to review every item of expenditure made upon the road. They exercised that right, and every item of expenditure was reviewed and approved by the Grand Trunk Pacific. Hon.

gentlemen opposite may say if they like- in fact, they have said-that the authorities of the Grand Trunk Pacific did not play fair with their principals. That is such a gross libel that I do not intend to argue it; but, assuming that the men responsible for the business of the Grand Trunk Pacific acted fairly by their principals, then their principals were protected, and this Dominion of Canada was equally protected by that provision in the contract, and there is no justification for the suggestion that there was unbusinesslike expenditure. Besides that, of the 21 contracts, not one-or hardly one-was completed and the money paid over until this Government came into power. This Government held the deposit money and the drawback money, and if they paid out money that should not have been paid out, they are responsible for it and not the late Government, and they must answer to the taxpayers of the Dominion of Canada for that payment.
I just wish to allude to a remark made by my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Boyce). He mentioned a resolution moved by the present leader of the Opposition on the presentation of a proposal by the Government of 1885 for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway short line between Montreal and St. John, in which the right hon. gentleman urged delay in order to get further surveys. My hon. friend drew a comparison between his urging delay on that occasion and his urging haste in presenting the Transcontinental railway proposal. Let me point out the difference. In the case of the short line between Montreal and St. John, the question was as to whether a line could or could not be got right through Canada. The right hon. gentleman was striving then for an allCanadian railway, just as he was in 1903, and it was in the hope that an all-Canadian line could be got that he asked for delay. I think it only right that the House should be informed on that point, because it is one of the strong points that the right hon. gentleman made when he introduced the proposal for the Transcontinental railway, namely, that we wanted an absolutely all-Canadian railway' from the Atlantic to the Pacific. If it has cost us money to have that, in the first place it was necessary that we as a country should have it; and, in the next place, if we are a country it is worth the having.
The construction of this line has been challenged because it ran through unknown country. Whether the country was known or unknown is not to the point. The point
is that by carrying this road, as it has been carried, from Quebec in 9 p.m. a direct line through Winnipeg and across the prairies to a port on the North Pacific, there has been created, so far as business interests are concerned, a new Quebec, a new Ontario, and new British Columbia out of areas of country that might as well have been in the centre of Africa so far as their material benefit to Canada was concerned without the construction of such a railway. The only criticism our friends opposite have to offer of this project is that we should have built it cheap whereas we have built it dear, that we should have built a temporary and inefficient road whereas we have built a permanent and efficient road, so far as they have allowed the work to go on.
In conclusion, whatever else may be charged against hon. gentlemen opposite they cannot be charged with inconsistency on the subject of opposition to the Transcontinental. In 1903 they fought it from midsummer until the snow flew. They fought it again in 1904. They have attempted, as best they could, to discredit it from that day to this, but it was only when they achieved power, when the enterprise fell into their hands, that they were able to carry into effect what they had wished to do from the very beginning. At this particular time, at this critical period in the history of the road, when vast sums of money have been sunk in its construction, at the moment when enormous further sums are required to absolutely complete and fully equip it, at a period during which traffic must be built up and development provided for the most critical period in the history of the road, our friends have seen fit to lay on the table of Parha-ment a report that has already been characterized as false, misleading, and an attempt to discredit in a business way the enterprise as well as to discredit politically this party. Their commissioners exhausted their ingenuity in finding cause to discredit the road and our friends in the House from day to day have repeated and emphasized everything that has been said in their report with that purpose in view. If ever this great enterprise can be wrecked they have chosen a favourable moment to use their influence as a party and as a government to wreck it by discrediting it as a business enterprise in the hope of discrediting their opponents on this side of the House. The report has been characterized as partisan. It is partisan; it is so partisan that it discredits itself.
