If I have not by my weak efforts been able to satisfy the curiosity of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, it is not my fault. I would refer him to the commissioners' report, and also to his compatriot, Mr. Mclsaac, K.C., from Nova Scotia. The Liberals, including the hon. member for North Cape Breton, are apparently not a little exercised over the publication of this report. And well they may be, for every argument and every criticism, and every statement in condemnation of this National Transcontinental road made by the Liberal-Conservative party in the past and by its leaders has been amply justified by this report. Every one who has followed the history of the construction of this line has, and has had for years, a strong suspicion that this construction was marked by plain, every day graft, maladministration and loose methods; and this 140
report amply justifies this suspicion. Consequently, we find the Liberals are in a white heat when discussing this report, as is evident in the case of the hon. member who interrupted me a moment ago. They do not discuss the merits of the Teport so much as attempt to attack the personnel of the commission. But the publication of the findings of this commission has roused such resentment and indignation throughout this country that should an -election be held at any early day, the Liberal party, once great, proud and haughty, but now reduced throughout the country to something of a remnant, would become a mere memory in the minds of the people.
Certain plausible reasons were given to the public why this road should be undertaken. We have heard them rehear-sed by the hon. ex-Minister of the Interior. They said the road was necessary in order to open new territory in the West and afford facilities for new settlements. But when the Grand Trunk was built in the We-s-t, it duplicated for miles and miles at a stretch the Canadian Pacific Tailway through the settled portions of the country. They told us that the construction of the road was necessary to Teduce the freight rates. But the tremendous cost resulting from incapacity, loose methods and lax administration have prevented the possibility of the reduction of freight rates in the time of this generation or the next. They said they wanted to open up the hinterland of Quebec and the Maritime provinces, and so they duplicated the Intercolonial railway; and no person to-day but the ex-Minister of the Interior has the temerity to justify that portion of the line. I give it as my opinion, after reading the report and the opinions of the engineers and of the late Hon. A. G. Blair, that language cannot be found to adequately characterize the folly, the criminal folly, of the late Government in building this portion of the line.
While certain ostensible reasons were given to the public why this road should be undertaken in the public interest, the people generally had grave suspicions that there were certain secret motives behind this construction. And the subsequent history of the work has justified these suspicions in the public mind. For instance, the people suspect that this road was projected as a monument to the present leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). The phenomenal success of the Canadian Pacific Tailway, which was inaugurated by Sir John A. Macdonald, has vindicated the

way (Canadian Pacific railway) from North Bay to Port William and make it a national highway of Canada and operate it hy means of an independent commission, giving to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern and the Intercolonial, as well as the Canadian Pacific railway, equal running power over it. I say that for this reason, that to build two railways, or three railways, where one railway, with running rights over it, will answer the same purpose, is economic waste.
These words should burn into the hearts of the Canadian people; because if this policy had been adopted there would be no occasion for the lamentable condition of affairs which exists to-day in connection with railway matters. The hon. exMinister of Eailways (Mr. Graham) is reported in the Ottawa Free Press of March 17, 1909, as saying:
Regarding the future of the Intercolonial, Mr. Graham frankly expressed the opinion that unless some arrangement were made so that line could ' hook-up ' and be made the outlet of a transcontinental line, it would find itself confined to the handling of local traffic, of which there was insufficient to maintain the road.
Seldom does the leader of any party find his arguments so readily endorsed as did the present Prime Minister in the statement made by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. In the election of 1904, would the people, if they had been able to brush aside the curtain of doubt and peer into the future, looking at the matter in the light of what has singe happened, have endorsed the policy that has been placed before them in the shape of the Grand Trunk Pacific, or would they have accepted the policy laid down by the present Prime Minister ? The people realize to-day as they never realized before that they have been deceived by the Liberal party, that they have been grossly robbed by the Liberal contractors, and that the construction of this road, as pointed out in the report of the commissioners, has been characterized by waste, extravagance and incapacity.
Many disasters have followed in the wake of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, The Hon. A. G. Blair was an able, far-seeing and constructive man. This road was built upon the political ruins of Mr. Blair; all that was mortal of this great man disappeared protesting against the tremendous folly of the Liberal party. Mr. Blair, humiliated by the action of his leader in negotiating this matter behind his back, against his wishes and contrary to his better judgment, protested to the bitter end against the policy of constructing the National Transcontinental railway. Mr. Blair was shorn of his honours as Minister

of Railways and Canals, yet, standing upon the floor of this House, towering in stature, in mental calibre, and in constructive genius away above other members of his party that surrounded him, he lashed and flayed his political friends in a manner which has had no parallel in this or any other Parliament. Like a prophet of old, in his righteous indignation he poured out the vials of his wrath upon his political friends, who were not only deceiving him, but were deceiving the people of this country as well. No such scathing arraignment of any policy or of any party or of any leader was ever recorded in history of any Parliament as that which was made on the floor of this House on August 11, 1903, when the Hon. A. G. Blair delivered his diatribe against the National Transcontinental railway. He said :
Why with such unusual and such unexampled haste a measure of this magnitude and this character had been pressed upon them. . . . What does the right hon. gentleman mean when he says: ' We cannot wait because time does not wait.' I think, Mr. Speaker, and I may sa^ it with all respect to my right hon. friend that it would have been as correct if not as poetic for him to have said; We cannot wait because Senator Cox cannot wait.
We find this stalwart of the Liberal party, an ex-Prime Minister of the province of New Brunswick, here representing a constituency of that province, condemning the whole eastern branch of the Transcontinental. He talks about the Government destroying its own property. He further says that when the Bill was under discussion in the Railway Committee, he asked Mr. Hays whether if the Government built down to Montreal, they might not arrange for an interchange of traffic and that Mr. Hays answered ' Yes, without any difficulty whatever.' Hon. Mr. Blair says:
The Intercolonial railway has been fully competent to take all the traffic that has been offered up to this date. . . . You will have the Government in the anomalous position of owning both roads, of operating one, and of being pratically interested in the successful operation of the other, going in and destroying its own property, impairing the value of its own property whether it he the one or the other, such a spectacle, I do not think, has ever been presented to the knowledge or observation of any human being since the world began.
I might repeat the sentence I read a moment ago in connection with what the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) said of the eastern branch from Quebec to Moncton. What does Mi. Blair say;

It is a total and absolute waste of public money. It is not only a destruction of the Intercolonial railway but it is a sheer unjusti-able squandering of the public money.
Could language be more severe? Could an argument be more irresistible or logic more deadly? Every paragraph, every sentence, every word that fell from the lips of Hon. A. G. Blair has come true, and the people of this country at last realize the real significance of that great man s opposition and hostility to this absurd, illogical and indefensible branch of the National Transcontinental railway. Disaster came not only to A. G. Blair, but also to Mr. Hodgins for opposing thi,s work. Mr. Hodgins was a man eminent in his profession and a Liberal in politics. Yet he was forced to acknowledge his inability to control the contractors along the line, his engineering staff, and the rapacious horde of Liberal heelers who wanted to make fortunes out of the road. What does he say. I quote from the Manitoba Free Press:
Hodgins charges enormous waste. Dismissed engineer declares millions are being stolen on Government section. Major's side of the story. States trouble first arose over question of c.assi-flcation. Ashed for investigation.
Alleging broadly that millions of dollars are being wasted or stolen in the construction of the Government portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway Major A. E. Hodgins, C.E., has issued a letter, the object of which is to secure an administrative investigation.
Major Hodgins is now a resident of Victoria. He is a son of Judge Hodgins, of Toronto, a Liberal, who recently demanded an investigation by the Government to inquire into the reason for his son's removal from office.
Was he a partisan?

I think we can designate
him a partisan according to the standard of the ex-Minister of the Interior. I say that Engineer Hodgins' charges have been substantiated and his reputation vindicated by the publication of the Gutelius-Staunton report, and no man in Canada to-day will welcome this report more than Engineer Hodgins and his friends.
In addition to them, we have Chief Engineer Lumsden, a man prominent an his profession, who by reason of, as he says in his letter of resignation, having lost all confidence in his engineering staff, also resigned from this road. His charges also have been substantiated and his reputation has been vindicated by this report. The Liberals may try to minimize the effect of charges made by Engineer Hodgins and Chief Engineer Lumsden, but there are certain salient and indisputable facts which
they cannot ignore. One of them is that these engineers had personal knowledge of what was happening in connection with this road; they made serious charges against the management of the road and the administration of the moneys spent, and in consequence they resigned. The third indisputable fact is that these charges have been substantiated, proved to the hilt, by the publication of this report. Those are the facts, notwithstanding that engineer Hodgins and chief engineer Lumsden were terrorized and intimidated more ot less to modify their charges before a certain partisan committee appointed to investigate them. Blair, Hodgins and Lumsden were victims of the ambition and greed of party friends of the Liberal party. They were mere pawns in the game, flies upon the wheel, and they were brushed unceremoniously aside in order that these men might pursue their course in becoming millionaires and multi-millionaires in a short time. With their knowledge, ideals and principles, these men were not wanted in the construction of this road; they were dismissed or their resignation demanded in older that the carnival of mismanagement might proceed unhindered. Hon. Mr. Blair foresaw what was coming and he washed his hands of the whole transaction. Hodgins and Lumsden actually saw what 10 p.m. the Hon. Mr. Blair foresaw, and they also washed their hands of the transaction. Engineers Hodgins and Lumsden held a post-mortem investigation, -perhaps I should say ante-mortem, because although the Grand Trunk Pacific is in extremis it has not yet utterly ex-pired,-which verified the predictions of Hon. Mr. Blair in regard to this road and confirmed the experience of Hodgins and Lumsden, who were men actually upon the work. Mr. Blair looked at this enterprise from the point of view of the future and condemned it; engineers Hodgins and Lumsden looked at it from the point of view of the present-men actually on the job- and they condemned it; commissioners Gutelius and Staunton looked at it from the point of view of the past and they condemned it. Hon. Mr. Blair has been reviled and execrated-one might almost say executed-<by the Liberal party. Engineers Hodgins and Lumsden were reviled and execrated by the Liberal party, so is it any wonder that they revile and execrate the names of Gutelius and Staunton?
This investigating commission was ideal for the purpose for which it was appointed.

It was composed of Mr. Gutelius, an expert railway engineer who was appointed to investigate and pass upon the engineering side of the enterprise, and of Mr. Staunton, an able and distinguished member of the Ontario bar whose duty it was to examine and cross-examine witnesses and report on the contracts. In their report, there is not a statement that is not supported to the hilt by the documentary evidence on file or by the sworn testimony of witnesses. AH those witnesses with the exception of one or two were the experts employed in the construction of the road. In other words the Liberal party have been convicted out of the mouths of their own employees. Every expression of opinion in that report is verified and amplified by the best expert opinion on the continent of North America. The very completeness of the report dumfounds hon. gentlemen opposite. They cannot successfully attack the merits of that report. The very completeness of it takes the Opposition, so to speak, at a disadvantage because they cannot successfully, either on questions of fact or of expert opinion, attack this report which has been so ably prepared by these commissioners. In this voluminous, exhaustive and unimpeachable report, these commissioners have placed upon the records of this House, and among the archives of this country, a document which not only vindicates the position taken by the Liberal-Conservative party in years past in respect to this enterprise, but which vindicates the judgment in the most flattering manner of the present right hon. Prime Minister in respect to this whole proposition. This report does more than vindicate the position of the Conservative party, it does more than vindicate the position of the Prime Minister; it exposes, in the minutest detail, and by the most incontrovertible evidence, the greatest piece of graft in the history of politics on the North American continent.
This gigantic waste need not surprise the Canadian mind when you consider the thoroughly political complexion of the former National Transcontinental Railway Commission. This commission was selected, not on account of its expert knowledge of railway construction and operation, but purely and simply on account of its knowledge of practical politics. It is most interesting to compare the methods which were employed by the United States Government in appointing a commission with the methods that obtained in Canada in appointing this 
commission for expending millions and millions of the people's money. At the time that the President of the United States appointed a commission to construct the Panama canal, did he appoint men such as the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals said that the Government had appointed-men of splendid ability but without any expert knowledge? Listen to the personnel of the commission appointed by the President of the United States: John G. Walker, rear-admiral of United States navy, who had been at the head of former canal commissions for purposes of investigation and report; Geo. W. Davis, a major-general of United States army, on the retired list; Wm. B. Parsons, an eminent civil engineer, of New York; Wm. H. Burr, professor of civil engineering in Columbia University of New York; Benj. M. Harrod, formerly city and state civil engineer of New Orleans; Carl E. Grusskey, civil engineer, of San Francisco; and Frank T. Hecker, a civil engineer, of Detroit.
With reference to that Panama canal matter, to what extent did the expenditure go beyond the estimate?
I have not the figures.
Everybody else has them.
Perhaps my hon. friend, having the knowledge, will give them to the House?
The expenditure was double the estimate.

Any person reading that can come to no other conclusion whatever than that a great amount of that money found its way into the political campaign fund of' the Liberal party.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I desire to say that the commissioners have thoroughly investigated this whole road; they have examined the contract; they have examined and cross-examined the witnesses and have made their report. They have summarized their findings in this significant paragraph:
We find that the Transcontinental Railway Commission, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and those having charge of the construction of the railway did not consider it desirable or necessary to practise or encourage economy in the construction of this road.
We find that without including the money which was unnecessarily expended in building the railway east of the St. Lawrence river $40,000,000 at least was needlessly expended in the building of this road.
Contrast that with the significant statement of the Hon. Mr. A. G. Blair. Speaking of the eastern branch of the National Transcontinental railroad, he said:
It is a total and absolute waste of the public money. It is not only a destruction of the Intercolonial railway, but it is a sheer unjustifiable squandering of the public money.
Had time permitted, I would have liked to go more in detail into the findings of the commission, because I never read in my life a more complete report, a report that proves the charges to the hilt out of the mouths of employees and witnesses belonging to the Liberal party. I believe that the people of Canada are at last seized of all the real facts in regard to this gigantic waste of $40,000,000, this Liberal masterpiece of wilful waste and wanton extravagance. When the opportunity is afforded them to register their protest, I venture to express the opinion that they will visit well-merited punishment upon the heads of those responsible for this national disgrace.

This is certainly the most important question that has been discussed in this House during the present session. It is more than that: it is the most important question to the people of this country and to this Government that has been discussed in this House for many years. The report of the Investigating Commission, Messrs. Lynch-Staunton and Gutelius, is bulky and technical. The discussion that has taken place upon it has been extensive and necessarily to a large extent of a technical character. It would therefore, in my opinion, be diffi-

cult for the ordinary man-even if he had *the time and inclination and opportunity to read this report and the discussion upon it and to follow them in .all their details- to come to a decision on the .question. There ought, however, to be some way for the plain citizen, the ordinary man, the ordinary taxpayer of this country, to grasp at least the fundamental features of the ease. I will endeavour to find that way and to follow it.
Before I do so, I want to draw the attention of the House /to this peculiar feature of the case. So far as we know, before this report was completed, before it was printed and laid on the table of the House, at all events before it was available to the members of the House, advance copies, exaggerated statements, biased statements, were given to the Conservative newspapers of the country, and. were published under flaming headlines. The attention of the country was called to the enormous graft that was about to be revealed, to the dishonesty that was about to be exposed. A superhuman effort almost was made to influence, inflame and prejudice .the country before the report saw the light of day at all. Was that a proper course to pursue? Were the men who were preparing this report afraid that, when the report was .submitted, it would not bear out the interpretation which they were sending out to- the country, and was it their intention that the country should be prejudiced first and the report submitted afterwards? It would certainly seem as if that was the case. If these men had confidence in the value of this report, they would have depended upon it to carry its story to the people.
I want to say a word or two with reference to the policy of the late Government, which has been called in question by this report, and which has been seriously called in question to-night by my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe). In 1903, when the Government of the country decided, in consequence of the development going on in the West and in consequence of the necessity of providing better and cheaper additional transportation facilities, upon building a railway from Winnipeg, Manitoba, to Moncton, New Brunswick, they decided to own it themselves and to connect it with a line of railway that the Grand Trunk Pacific would build from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. Every province in the Dominion of Canada was to benefit from the construction and operation of this railway. It was to be truly a national transcontinental railway. We know that the Conservative

party at that time was in favour of this railway stopping at Cochrane, and of sending the traffic and the business that would come over it from the West to Toronto and from there through United States territory to United States ports. Some of them wished the railway to be carried as far as Quebec, but no one wished it to go into the Maritime provinces, and from Quebec the freight was to be diverted to Portland. The Maritime provinces were to be left out of the reckoning altogether. We might pay our share of the cost, but were to receive none of the advantages. That was the policy of the Opposition at that time and it is still the policy of the Conservative party. The Government of that day thought and acted differently. On the question of policy they went to the people in 1904 and again in 1908, and the people endorsed that policy. It is just possible that the late Government and the Liberal party and the majority of the people of Canada were as well qualified to pronounce an opinion upon the proper policy to be pursued in that respect as Mr. Gutelius or Mr. Lynch-Staunton or the Conservative party or even my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe). When a policy was decided upon, it was also decided, as has been pointed out time and again, that a railway of the best standard in America would be constructed, so that the operating expenses of the road would be as light as possible, and so that it would be a true competing line with the Canadian Pacific railway or any other railway in Canada.
What was the arrangement entered into with the Grand Trunk Pacific? While the Government was to build from Winnipeg to Moncton, the Gnand Trunk Pacific was to build from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. The Grand Trunk Pacific, with the guarantee of the Grand Trunk railway, a large and wealthy railway corporation, agreed to take over the road when constructed by the Government, under a lease for fifty years, and pay 3 per cent upon the cost of construction, whatever it might be, for forty-three years out of the fifty, to operate the road and provide the betterments, that is, to keep it in proper repair. Therefore, it was to the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk railway that this road should be built honestly and economically. They had the right and privilege and duty of putting their engineers on the road while it was under construction, to see to it that every dollar was properly expended; and they did that. What better arrangement
could be made to insure honesty and economy? I do not think the ingenuity of man could devise a better arrangement. Then the commission wias appointed consisting of four men. The Government of to-day is trying to smirch the reputation of these mm. But these men .are reputable Canadian citizens, and I do not think the efforts of the Government should be directed towards destroying their reputation. That commission had the .advantage of being .assisted .by the best engineers who could be found in Canada. If graft has been carried on, that commission must have been dishonest; the engineers employed by them and paid by the people of this country must have been dishonest; the engineers employed by the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk railway must have been in collusion with the grafters, and they also must have been dishonest; and the contractors must have been dishonest. Mr. Speaker, if all those .safeguards have broken down and this dishonesty has taken place, there must be something inherently wrong with the people of Canada, for it would be impossible to devise better safeguards to insure the honesty of a public work.
Now, we come to another feature of. this case, and a serious one for this Government. I said a moment ago that it would be difficult for the ordinary man to wade through this mass of evidence prepared by lawyers and engineers, and to discover who was right and who was wrong. But it is easy for the ordinary man to see that if all this graft that is charged has taken place, all these men whom I have mentioned must be guilty. This Government is the guardian and custodian of the public funds. What is the Government going to do about it? Is it going to prosecute any of those who are represented to us as rascals, the parties to this huge graft, all this enormous thieving, when millions of the public money were squandered-forty millions, according to this report, squandered and several millions dishonestly taken? I see a member of the Government present, the Hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen); does he think this Government has no responsibility in this matter? Not only have they not started any prosecutions against the men who are alleged to have done these things, but they have retained these same men, these engineers, in their service. Now, this Government is not very sensitive in regard to dismissals; their conscience is not tender upon that point; they have dismissed men

for the most trivial reasons. They have dismissed men simply because they were suspected of being Liberals when there was no other charge against them. They have dismissed men from the post office, from the customs, from the lighthouses, from the railways, simply because they were Liberals, though these were honest men, faithfully discharging their public duties. Why, they have dismissed men who were dead because it was believed they were Liberals; they have dismissed men simply because the/ patted a Liberal dog on the street. But, according to their own statement, here are men in the employ of the Government'who have assisted in robbing the people of this country of millions of dollars-and not even one of them dismissed. If that report be true and the statements made by the members who have spoken on the opposite side be true, this Government is aiding, abetting and shielding rascals and is equally guilty with them. That is what the people who pay their taxes want to know, and the Government are not going to get away from that. If what is alleged on the Government side be true, these men should not be at large; the penitentiary is the place for them. Again I say: What is the Government going to do about it ?
But there is more than that in it. If one-tenth part of what is charged by the members on the other side has taken place, the contractors themselves are dishonest men. When this Government came into power they found that a deposit had been made by every one of these contractors; they had also in their possession a drawback kept by the late Government. Had this Government been sincere in this matter, they should have retained that money until this business was cleared up. These contractors had solemnly agreed faithfully and honestly to carry out their contracts under forfeit of the money that they had placed in the hands of the Government as a guarantee. But this Government exacts nothing; they have paid out that money in many instances without exacting a dollar. But they have done more than that. During the time the late Government were in power, a dispute arose between the Government engineers and the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and that dispute was referred to arbitration under the provisions of the statute. The arbitrators were: For the Grand Trunk Pacific, Mr. Kelliher; for the Transcontinental Commission-that is for the Government-Mr. Gordon Grant; and the third arbitrator, Mr. Colling-wood Schreiber. The arbitrators de-EMr. J. J. Hughes.]
cided that they would deduct from the claim of J. D. McArthur the sum of $550,000, and the late Government decided to carry out that award. What did this Government do since they came into power? They set aside the award of the arbitrators and deducted only $150,000 from the account, thus paying this contractor $400,000 more than the arbitrators had said he was entitled to, and more than the late Government had decided to give him. In the face of that, can this Government dare charge the late Administration or the Transcontinental Commission with not doing their duty, or with not guarding the public funds? The taxpayers of this country will have to know why the finding of the arbitration board was overruled, and why $400,000 of the people's money was paid out to this contractor. Yet we are asked to believe that it was the late Government, or the Transcontinental Commission, that was squandering the public money.
I do not know, I cannot conceive, how this Government can tell the people of the country that they knew that certain men had robbed the taxpayers, and yet kept them in their service; that they did not prosecute them, did not take legal proceedings against them, but condoned everything. I do not think that such a record was ever made in the history of Canada or of any other country. When the Liberal party made charges against men tor squandering public money- against Connolly and McGreevy, for instance-they took these men into the courts and exposed and punished them. They gave a reason for the faith that was in them; they acted properly and like men, and if there is any truth in this report the present Government should act in the same way. But hon. gentlemen opposite know that the report is not true; they do not believe it themselves; and they have not acted upon a single finding of the report from the time they received it until the present day.
The Government, at enormous expense to the country, employed two men to investigate this matter. These men prepared a report, and, if it ibe not true-and we are driven to that conclusion-then it is a slanderous report, which is being circulated by the Government throughout the country. 1 do not profess to know anything about the law, but the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) said that one of the members of the commission,

Mr. Lyn-ch-Staunton, was one of the most distinguished members of the Ontario bar, Mr. Lyneh-Staunton had an opinion, which he published in that report, and the Minister of Justice and the Deputy Minister of Justice, over their own signatures, said that he was all wrong-that his larw was no good. Yet the Government is spending tens of thousands of dollars to circulate that false report throughout the country for the purpose of prejudicing the public mind. I have shown you, Mr. Speaker, how hon. gentlemen opposite agree on a point of law; that is the opinion they have of Mr. Lynch-Staunton's knowledge. I think that is the way the taxpayers of this country will look at this question. I repeat that the commissioners employed by this Government have made a report in which they charge that enormous sums of money have been misappropriated. The persons who are alleged to be guilty are all in this country; many of them are in the employ of the Government; yet the Government is taking no action whatever to punish these men for their alleged misdeeds. If this report be true, we have an instance of the greatest miscarriage of justice on the part of the Government that ever took place in this or iany other country. Will the people of Canada stand for that kind of thing? If the Teport be not true, then it is the most slanderous document that has ever been given to the people of Canada-and it has been produced under the auspices of this Government. I would like to ask the ministers who are present to-night what further action they intend to take. This matter should not be allowed to rest here; further investigations should take place for the protection of the people; further examination into the matter should be made if ttie Government have not enough information to enable them to proceed against the guilty parties. Is that not common sense; is that not ordinary reason? The people of this country will ask for it, they have a right to ask for it, and if they get justice their demands will be satisfied; but they will not get justice. The interests of the people are not considered in this matter; the whole thing appears to have been conspiracy which was entered into for the purpose of discrediting the late Government, for the purpose of discrediting the Liberal party, for the purpose of degrading the Transcontinental railway, regardless of consequences. No amount of special pleading, no amount of finely-spun arguments, no amount of covering up, will keep these
patent facts away from the minds of the people. One man perhaps more than all the others is responsible for this condition of affairs, and that man in the last 'analysis is the right hon. the Prime Minister. On him the responsibility must rest.
One of the points of this commission's report is -that if we had built a cheaper road it would not have -cost -so much. We had to pay $65,000 in order to get that valuable piece of information. Mr. Gutelius says it is unnecessary for the Grand Trunk Pacific to have a level or a straight road, but he would like exceedingly well to induce -the Government of this country to give -him money to take the lumps out of the Intercolonial and make it reasonably straight. He says he could operate the Intercolonial much more cheaply if that were done; but he reports that it is not necessary for the Transcontinental. Any ordinary man can -see some flaw in that reasoning. I say again, the whole thing seems to have -been a conspiracy to discredit the Liberal party and to degrade the Transcontinental. Is it possible that that was intentionally done so that the Grand Trunk Pacific should not take over this road when it was completed; so that it should be handed over to- some other company, the Canadian Pacific railway for instance and the people of Canada would he deprived of competition in transportation? The President of the Grand Trunk Pacific, Mr. Chamberlin, has already notified the Government -that he might not take it over if they went on degrading the road as they were doing-he would not hold himself responsible for the operation of the road. No government in this country ever occupied a more untenable or more unreasonable position-a position more in direct opposition to the best interests of the people-than this one.
